extracted.subtask_description: A university library research guide describing real-world plagiarism scandals, the consequences of plagiarism, and concrete practices students should follow to avoid plagiarizing in research papers, theses, and journalistic writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate source credibility and author qualifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Always make sure to evaluate your sources! Find out who the author is and what their background is in the topic they're writing about. Why are they qualified to write on this topic?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify author expertise and appropriateness of the source for your assignment. Example/anti-pattern: UNC football receiver Erik Highsmith posted blog content taken from other websites (including content written by 11-year-olds) — showing failure to check source suitability/authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rushing/procrastination
rubrics_metrics.description: These players may have also been in a hurry to turn in their assignments. Take your time, as procrastination may make you more likely to plagiarize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan and allow sufficient time for research and writing; rushing increases the risk of copying without proper attribution. Example: student-athletes under time pressure may submit plagiarized work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful note-taking: mark quotes vs. paraphrase and record page numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful when you're taking notes! Make it clear where you have quoted the original source, and where you have paraphrased, and always include page numbers so you can go back and double check your work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clear note conventions (e.g., quotation marks, labelled paraphrase notes, page citations) to avoid accidental plagiarism. Example: Fareed Zakaria said the mistake occurred when he confused notes taken about different sources — proper tracking would prevent such confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Always attribute and cite sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicate when material is quoted or paraphrased and provide full citation information so original authors are credited and readers can verify sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistently use the citation style required (APA/MLA/etc.) and include page numbers for direct quotes. Failure to attribute leads to accusations of plagiarism and can damage reputation (e.g., journalists suspended or publications harmed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid self-plagiarism; get permission to reuse your prior work
rubrics_metrics.description: Yes, you can plagiarize yourself. Even if it's your own work, if you try to pass it off a second time as something 'original,' you're being dishonest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you want to reuse work from another course or prior publication, discuss it with your instructor/editor and obtain permission or provide proper citation/acknowledgement. Example: Jonah Lehrer republished his own work across outlets (self-plagiarism) and faced professional consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not fabricate quotes or data; ensure accuracy of attributed material
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not invent or attribute false quotes or facts to sources or people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify primary source material before quoting; fabrication (e.g., Lehrer making up quotes attributed to Bob Dylan) can lead to investigations, resignations, and retractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid copying large sections; properly attribute translations, tables, and charts
rubrics_metrics.description: A thesis or paper must meet professional and ethical standards; extensive verbatim copying, identical translations, or uncredited tables/charts constitutes serious plagiarism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paraphrase substantively or use quotation and citation for any copied text, and obtain permission/credit for reproduced tables/figures. Examples: Pal Schmitt and Karl-Theodor zu Guttenberg had major portions of doctoral theses identical to other works (including translations and copied tables), resulting in degree revocation and resignations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the possible consequences of plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: People caught plagiarizing may face academic probation, suspension from job, forced job resignation, being stripped of degree, bans from postseason play, suspension from publications, and long-term reputational harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the seriousness of plagiarism through real-world examples: NCAA sanctions (UNC football players), suspensions from Time/CNN (Fareed Zakaria temporarily), resignations and degree revocations (Pal Schmitt, Karl-Theodor zu Guttenberg), and professional fallout from fabricated or plagiarized journalism (Jonah Lehrer). Use these examples as deterrents and motivation to follow ethical practices.
